title: The Waitress Is Getting Married

jokes.text: Dee complaining that the wedding dress is 'doing nothing for my hip area and making a mess of my boobs' while trying on dresses she has no wedding for
jokes.setup: Dee is in a bridal shop, ostensibly shopping for a wedding dress
jokes.punchline: Her complaint is entirely about vanity/appearance — she has no actual wedding planned, making the criticism absurdly self-focused
jokes.explanation: Establishes Dee's narcissism immediately — she's focused on her appearance, not the absurdity of her situation. Functional opener but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: What do you think? It's kind of doing nothing for my hip area and making a mess of my boobs.

jokes.text: The bridal shop worker confronts Dee: she's been coming in every Saturday for over a year trying on dresses with no actual wedding planned
jokes.setup: Dee is acting like a normal bridal customer, asking for more dresses
jokes.punchline: The worker reveals Dee has been doing this compulsively for over a year — she is a sad, delusional regular at a bridal shop
jokes.explanation: Strong character-revealing joke. The reveal that Dee has been pathetically trying on wedding dresses every Saturday for a year is a sharp, economical way to establish her desperation without exposition. Character-specific and cringe-inducing in the best Sunny tradition.

dialogue.speaker: Store Employee
dialogue.line: Because you've been coming in here and trying on wedding dresses every saturday for over a year now.

jokes.text: 'Don't get up all over my balls, Lucy. Just go get the dresses.'
jokes.setup: The shop worker is pressing Dee for proof of a wedding
jokes.punchline: Dee responds with a weirdly aggressive, crude dismissal ('get up all over my balls') as if she is the one being wronged here
jokes.explanation: Classic Dee entitlement — she's being caught in a pathetic lie but doubles down with crude aggression. The specific phrasing 'get up all over my balls' is oddly quotable and character-consistent.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Don't get up all over my balls, Lucy, just go get the dresses.

jokes.text: Dee's escalating lies under questioning: vague wedding location ('the nearby church... right down the street'), fiance named 'Sam' who does 'sea... salt... he's a salt seaman'
jokes.setup: The shop worker interrogates Dee about her supposed upcoming wedding with rapid-fire questions
jokes.punchline: Each answer is vaguer and more desperate than the last, culminating in the absurd invention of a 'salt seaman' who dives for sea salt
jokes.explanation: Excellently structured escalating lie sequence. The rhythm of the rapid-fire Q&A — each answer more desperate and nonsensical than the last — is perfectly constructed. 'S-S-Salt... sea salt... he's a salt seaman... he dives into the ocean for the sea salt and then he brings it back up and then we eat it' is a masterclass in comedic escalation. The structure alone earns this high marks, and it's deeply character-specific to Dee's particular brand of delusional, flailing self-sabotage.

dialogue.speaker: Store Employee
dialogue.line: What is your fiance's name?

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Sam.

dialogue.speaker: Store Employee
dialogue.line: What is he do?

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: S... Salt. Salt? Sea salt. Sea salt. He's a salt... Seaman. He dives into the ocean for the sea salt, and then he brings it back up and then, we eat it.

jokes.text: Brad Fisher recognizes Dee and says she looks 'amazing' — Dee's response: 'Your acne cleared up really well.'
jokes.setup: Brad gives Dee a genuine compliment about how good she looks
jokes.punchline: Dee returns with a backhanded non-compliment about his acne having cleared up — inadvertently revealing she only found him repulsive before
jokes.explanation: Economical and character-true — Dee thinks she's flirting but immediately insults him, perfectly encapsulating how terrible she is at human interaction. The line does double duty: establishes Dee's social incompetence AND the acne backstory.

dialogue.speaker: Brad
dialogue.line: Your acne cleared up really well!

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: It was because of the acne. Yes, when i got real bad, you dumped me and you said it was because i was gonna grow up to look like Edward James Olmos.

jokes.text: Brad reveals Dee specifically said he would 'grow up to look like Edward James Olmos' when she dumped him
jokes.setup: Dee claims she doesn't remember exactly why she dumped him
jokes.punchline: He corrects her with the specific, humiliating detail that she told him he'd look like Edward James Olmos — a memorably specific and cruel put-down
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Edward James Olmos' elevates what could be a generic acne joke into something genuinely funny and memorable. It's such a specific, cruel, and oddly precise thing for a teenager to say. Works as both a character joke about teenage Dee's cruelty and a solid standalone line.

dialogue.speaker: Brad
dialogue.line: So you're getting married, wow!

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Yes. No, i'm not. This is because i was. But that didn't work out.

jokes.text: Brad calls over his fiancée to meet Dee — it's the waitress. Dee's jaw-drop reaction shot (implied by the 'Oh, my God' at 02:09 and the extended silent beat until 02:46).
jokes.setup: Brad is engaged, Dee has been flirting with him, he calls his fiancée over
jokes.punchline: The fiancée is the waitress — Charlie's obsession and the episode's title character — landing as a double shock (Dee's romantic hope crushed AND the episode's central conflict introduced simultaneously)
jokes.explanation: Structurally elegant cold open payoff. The scene has been building toward Dee's potential reconnection with Brad, then pulls the rug out in a way that simultaneously establishes the entire episode's premise. The long silent beat (nearly 40 seconds until the next scene at 02:46) is the joke — Dee's inability to process this in the bridal shop she's been haunting for a year. Economically brilliant storytelling.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Oh my god!

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis trying to safely move a buzzing box of bees into the basement for honey — 'Well, I'm fine with the bees. It's the honey I don't want to agitate.'
jokes.setup: Mac has apparently acquired a beehive to keep in the bar basement for free honey
jokes.punchline: Dennis draws a distinction between agitating the bees (fine) vs. agitating the honey (not fine), which is backwards and nonsensical
jokes.explanation: Solid absurdist aside — Dennis's inverted logic about honey vs. bees gets a chuckle but isn't deeply character-specific. Any idiot in any show could say this.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I'm fine with the bees. It's the honey i don't wanna agitate.

jokes.text: Mac sees a wasp, panics that it's not a bee — 'Is this a wasp nest? This is a wasp nest. I'm out!' — but Dennis stays to investigate if wasps make something delicious
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are already nervous about the bees/hornets
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately abandons the plan at the sight of a wasp, but Dennis's reasoning for staying is that wasps might make 'something delicious' — his greed overrides his self-preservation
jokes.explanation: 'There could be something delicious in here that wasps do make, and I want that' is a funny line but slightly undercut by being one of several bee/wasp/hornet beats in rapid succession.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: We always have bees is what we always have.

jokes.text: Frank's 'booty call' has been screaming in pain from a sting/something; Frank tells her 'Put some vegetable oil on it. That'll make you feel better. Okay. Bye, sexy.'
jokes.setup: Someone is screaming in pain off-screen
jokes.punchline: Frank dismisses them with 'bye, sexy' and the reveal that this screaming person is his booty call — establishing Frank's complete indifference to partners' pain as a character note
jokes.explanation: Frank's casual cruelty is on-brand. Brief but effective. 'Bye, sexy' as a farewell to a screaming, potentially injured person is a solid dark beat.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Do wasp make honey? No, wasps do not make honey.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I'm gonna check it out anyway. There could be something delicious in here that wasp do make. I want that.

jokes.text: 'That's my booty call. We're into some really weird food fetish stuff.'
jokes.setup: Mac/Dennis ask who that (screaming person) was
jokes.punchline: Frank explains it's his booty call and they're into 'weird food fetish stuff' — delivered with zero self-consciousness as if this is perfectly normal
jokes.explanation: Economic and character-perfect. The 'really weird food fetish stuff' as a throwaway line from Frank — delivered with no shame — is funny precisely because we don't get elaboration. Sets up later Artemis/bacon bits payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Am i a bad boy? I'm a bad boy? Put some vegetable oil on it. That'll make you feel better. Okay. Bye, sexy.

jokes.text: Mac reveals the waitress is getting married. Dennis: 'She doesn't seem to get our sense of humor. We do stuff that I think's funny. She doesn't. Hilarious!'
jokes.setup: Dee brings up the problem of the waitress getting married; Dennis dismisses caring about it
jokes.punchline: Dennis's defense of the gang's behavior is that they 'do stuff that I think's funny' — a perfect encapsulation of his narcissistic solipsism, delivered with zero self-awareness
jokes.explanation: Dennis characterizing the gang's harassment of the waitress as 'stuff that I think's funny' with no awareness that she's the victim is a sharp character moment. 'Hilarious!' as a kicker is well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: That's my booty call, we're into some really weird food fetish stuff.

jokes.text: Mac's theory: Dee doesn't care about Charlie — she's afraid Charlie will 'blow his brains out' and she'd 'have to do all the Charlie work'
jokes.setup: Dee claims she's worried about Charlie finding out about the wedding
jokes.punchline: Mac cuts through to the real reason: Dee is selfishly afraid of the increased workload if Charlie kills himself, not genuinely concerned for him
jokes.explanation: 'Do all the Charlie work' is a great phrase — it treats Charlie's potential suicide as primarily a staffing problem. Dark, economical, and perfectly Sunny in its casual nihilism.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You don't give a shit about Charlie, all your care about is that the waitress is getting married before you.

jokes.text: Dee's three-part selfishness speech: 'A: I do not want to do Charlie's work once he kills himself. B: How could the waitress get married before me? I'm way hotter than she is. And C: The guy she's marrying used to be my boyfriend.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Frank correctly call out Dee's real motivations for caring about the wedding
jokes.punchline: Dee confirms all of it in a perfectly structured three-part confession that reveals her narcissism, competitiveness, and wounded ego — the last point (C) being the new explosive reveal
jokes.explanation: The A/B/C structure is a classic comedy device but executed with real craft here. Each item escalates the horror of Dee's character: (A) acknowledges suicidal ideation as an inconvenience, (B) is petty competitiveness, (C) is the bombshell that explains the whole cold open. Dee confirming everything the gang assumed about her — without shame — is a great character-comedy beat.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: A) I don't wanna do Charlie's work once he kills himself. B) How could the waitress getting married before me? I'm way hotter than she is. And C) Get this, the guy she's marrying used to be my boyfriend.

jokes.text: 'You know what I just realized? I don't care about anything she's saying. Not a bit.'
jokes.setup: Dee has just revealed the explosive C point (Brad is her ex)
jokes.punchline: Dennis flatly announces mid-sentence that he has tuned out entirely and doesn't care about anything Dee said
jokes.explanation: The timing is sharp — Dennis has heard a legitimately dramatic reveal and his response is complete indifference. Very Dennis. Economical and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I'm trying to smoke these hornets to death so i can get their honey, but they keep flying up the tube, stinging me on my face and I think I just swallowed one.

jokes.text: The gang's solution to Charlie's potential violence: 'Get him his own booty call' / 'Or at least another chick to stalk'
jokes.setup: The gang is genuinely worried Charlie might 'go postal' and kill them all if he finds out
jokes.punchline: Their solution is to get him 'another chick to stalk' — treating stalking as a normal, redirectable behavior rather than something to address
jokes.explanation: 'Another chick to stalk' as a euphemism for 'distraction' is darkly funny — the gang normalizing Charlie's stalking behavior as a manageable personality quirk rather than something alarming.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Let me pop a quick H on this box, this way we all know that it's filled with hornets.

jokes.text: Charlie is in the bar, face covered in stings, with a tube/smoker trying to smoke hornets to death: 'They keep flying up the tube, stinging me on my face. I think I just swallowed one.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis find Charlie supposedly just doing bar work
jokes.punchline: Charlie has escalated his wasp/hornet situation to the point of being swarmed and stung on his face, yet is determined to continue; casually mentions he swallowed one
jokes.explanation: 'I think I just swallowed one' delivered as an aside to the main conversation is very Charlie — his physical suffering is secondary to his goal. The visual of Charlie's stung-up face throughout the episode is a running physical gag.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: What if I wore a checkered hat and smoked a pipe? You know, for the Sherlock Holmes look.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Why would you want to look like Sherlock Holmes?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Who are you trying to attract exactly?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Intelligent women.

jokes.text: 'I just don't think there's any science to support that, buddy.' — Charlie insisting hornets make honey despite all evidence
jokes.setup: Dennis explains (correctly) that you cannot get honey from hornets
jokes.punchline: Charlie dismisses an established scientific fact as an unsupported claim, delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Charlie's stubborn rejection of basic science in favor of wishful thinking is very character-specific. 'I just don't think there's any science to support that' about a universally known fact is a great Charlie line.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Milksteak.

jokes.text: Charlie marks the hornet box with an 'H' so everyone knows it's hornets. 'Let me pop a quick H on this box. This way we all know it's filled with the hornets.'
jokes.setup: Dennis and Mac are trying to redirect Charlie to the dating profile
jokes.punchline: Charlie pauses the conversation to thoughtfully label the hornet box — treating a dangerous pest problem with the organizational instincts of a practical person, which he is not in any other area of life
jokes.explanation: Charlie's practical gesture in an absurd situation is funny. 'This way we all know it's filled with the hornets' is unnecessary explanation that adds to the comedy — as if someone might wonder what the H stands for.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Milksteak.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Milksteak.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I'm not putting milksteak. Just put steak.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Don't put steak, put milksteak. She'll know what it is.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: No she won't know what it is, Charlie. Nobody knows what that is.

jokes.text: Charlie wants to look like Sherlock Holmes — checkered hat and pipe — for his dating profile photo 'to attract intelligent women'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis want a simple profile photo; Charlie asks about makeup
jokes.punchline: Charlie's alternative to makeup is Sherlock Holmes cosplay, which he believes will attract intelligent women — the gap between his self-image and reality is enormous
jokes.explanation: Very Charlie — his aspirational self-image (intellectual, pipe-smoking detective) vs. the reality (barely literate janitor covered in hornet stings) is a perfect character gap. 'To attract intelligent women' as the stated goal lands especially well given the context.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Magnets.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Okay, what, making magnets? Collecting magnets? Playing with magnets? Just magnets.

jokes.text: Charlie's favorite food: 'Milk steak.' Mac and Dennis's horrified reaction and attempt to substitute 'steak'
jokes.setup: Dennis asks Charlie for his favorite food for the dating profile
jokes.punchline: 'Milk steak' — an invented, incoherent dish — delivered with total confidence, while Dennis and Mac scramble to make it sound normal
jokes.explanation: One of the most iconic lines in It's Always Sunny history. 'Milk steak' is two words that have no business being together, yet Charlie says it with the confidence of someone naming a beloved dish. The payoff — 'She'll know what it is' (she won't, nobody will) — adds another layer. This is a cultural touchstone for the show, referenced in fan culture for years. Perfect character integration: only Charlie could have a favorite food called milk steak. Near-perfect economy — two words do enormous comedic work. Comparable in quotability and cultural impact to the calibration anchors provided.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Ghouls. You know, funny little green ghouls. Little green ghouls, buddy!

jokes.text: Charlie's hobby: 'Ghouls.' 'You know, funny little green ghouls, go-' Mac: 'What?!'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are already reeling from 'magnets' and ask for more hobbies
jokes.punchline: 'Ghouls' — specifically 'funny little green ghouls' — as a listed hobby, with Charlie beginning to describe them as if Mac just needs more detail to understand
jokes.explanation: Escalates perfectly from 'magnets.' Mac's 'Son of a bitch' and 'What are you talking about now?' are the right straight-man reactions. 'Funny little green ghouls' as a specific subcategory that Charlie thinks clarifies things is excellent. The partial description ('go-') suggesting Charlie was about to elaborate on what ghouls do adds another layer. Part of a legendary sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: People's knees. Cover your knees up if you're gonna be walking around everywhere.

jokes.text: Charlie's dislike: 'People's knees.' Dennis: 'Come on! Come on! You gotta be kidding me.'
jokes.setup: Dennis asks for dislikes, hoping for something usable like 'traffic' or 'rude people'
jokes.punchline: 'People's knees' — a hyper-specific, inexplicably targeted aversion to a body part — which Dennis cannot even begin to work with
jokes.explanation: The triumphant finish to the dating profile sequence. 'People's knees' as a dislike is so specific and unexplained that it becomes funnier the more you think about it — why knees? Just knees? Dennis's complete breakdown ('Come on! Come on! You gotta be kidding!') is the perfect reactive punctuation. 'Cover your knees up if you're gonna be walking around everywhere' as the kicker adds a callback logic to Charlie's worldview. Excellent economy and character work.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Bingo, bitch!

jokes.text: 'Bingo, bitch.' — Dee spots Brad and the waitress on the street from her car
jokes.setup: Dee has been scheming to sabotage the wedding by luring Brad away
jokes.punchline: 'Bingo, bitch' as a triumphant one-liner — Dee congratulating herself with trashy confidence while embarking on a scheme that will obviously fail
jokes.explanation: Short, punchy, character-consistent. The gap between Dee's self-satisfaction and the reality of her situation is the joke. Quotable in context.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I was thinking since Brad you were saying how your wedding was gonna be poor,boring or dull...

dialogue.speaker: Brad
dialogue.line: Did you say our wedding was gonna be dull?

dialogue.speaker: Brad
dialogue.line: I said it was gonna be small.

jokes.text: Dee yells at traffic from the car while trying to pitch a bachelorette party to Brad and the waitress, repeatedly insulting drivers ('calm down, dick wads')
jokes.setup: Dee is trying to make a smooth, friendly pitch to Brad and the waitress from her car window
jokes.punchline: The scene is constantly interrupted by honking — Dee is blocking traffic — and she pivots between faux-cheerful charm offensive and screaming insults at drivers
jokes.explanation: Classic cringe setup — Dee trying to be charming while creating a public disturbance. The 'Is it a yes or a no? 'Cause you're kinda holding up traffic here. It's rude.' line is a nice inversion where she calls out the rudeness she's causing.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: We like to put 'em in Artemis's hair and they rain down on me when we bang. I feel like a Cobb salad. It's amazing.

jokes.text: Frank wants 'bacon bits' for Artemis's hair so they 'rain down on me when we bang. I feel like a Cobb salad.'
jokes.setup: Frank asks Dee for bacon bits seemingly out of nowhere
jokes.punchline: Frank explains the bacon bits are for a sexual food fetish with Artemis — specifically he wants to feel like a Cobb salad during sex
jokes.explanation: Callback payoff on the food fetish setup, and it exceeds expectations. 'I feel like a Cobb salad' is a genuinely inspired, deeply weird line — the specificity of the salad type (Cobb, not just 'a salad') is crucial. Only Frank Reynolds could want to feel like a Cobb salad during sex and describe it with such earnest satisfaction. High originality, excellent character integration, beautifully economical. Among the episode's best lines.

dialogue.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
dialogue.line: Nobody hurts my Charlie.

jokes.text: Dee bribes Mrs. Mac with cigarettes to say the waitress 'looks exactly like you when you were young'
jokes.setup: Dee is staging the bachelorette party to sabotage the waitress's relationship
jokes.punchline: The 'bribe' is a carton of cigarettes — the currency of the elderly and desperate — and Mrs. Mac is immediately compliant
jokes.explanation: Functional setup joke establishing the party sabotage. The cigarette bribe is economical but not especially original.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I thought there was like cocain and heroin, and remember when you were shooting out with the homeless people and banging for money on the street.

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: No, wow you're making all of that up.

jokes.text: Dee tells Mrs. Kelly 'this man I'm bringing over wants to steal the love of your son's life away' — Mrs. Kelly: 'Nobody hurts my Charlie!'
jokes.setup: Dee is prepping Mrs. Kelly to be hostile at the party
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Kelly responds with fierce maternal protectiveness — but the joke is that she's being manipulated into a party game by Dee, and her sincerity makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: Setup beat — Mrs. Kelly's protectiveness will pay off at the party. Functional but not exceptional on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You're a philanthropist, that's what you are. You used to on a small business, but you gave all they up to help others. Who do i help? Who am i helping? It doesn't matter. I don't know, old people, children autistics, dyslexic folks...

jokes.text: Dee calls the waitress a 'big, old, fat stick in the mud' as a greeting
jokes.setup: The waitress arrives clearly not wanting to be there
jokes.punchline: Dee greets her with a cheery 'big, old, fat stick in the mud!' — an insult dressed up as affectionate teasing, completely inappropriate for someone she's supposed to be warming up to
jokes.explanation: Classic Dee self-sabotage — she's trying to be charming but can't help insulting people. Functional but not especially sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You're a philanthropist

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I'm a flan...

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Phi-lan-thro-pist

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Philanthropist!

jokes.text: Dee tells the waitress the punch has no alcohol — 'No, absolutely not. I remember what an embarrassing problem you have with alcohol.' — then immediately tries to tell Brad about her 'unfortunate problems with drugs and alcohol'
jokes.setup: The waitress asks if the punch has alcohol; Dee says no with fake concern
jokes.punchline: Dee immediately weaponizes this 'concern' by loudly broadcasting the waitress's drinking problem to Brad — the fake kindness revealed as pure manipulation in the same breath
jokes.explanation: Good cringe structure — the pivot from fake concern to sabotage attempt happens within seconds. Dee's particular flavor of cruelty (disguised as helpfulness) is well-executed here.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: How much cheese have you eaten today? How much cheese is too much cheese? Any amount of cheese before a date is too much cheese.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I had a lot of cheese. I had a block of cheese.

jokes.text: Dee escalates to 'remember when you were shooting up with the homeless people and banging for money on the street?'
jokes.setup: Dee is trying to discredit the waitress in front of Brad by exaggerating her drinking problem
jokes.punchline: Dee's story escalates from 'alcohol problem' to 'heroin' to 'shooting up with homeless people and banging for money' — a grotesque overreach that she delivers as if reading from memory
jokes.explanation: Good escalation joke — Dee goes from 'drinking problem' to full street-level prostitution and heroin use in one breath, which is both funny in its excess and revealing of Dee's desperation and cruelty.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Who broke Brad's heart in high school and feels really bad about it?

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: Me. I broke Brad's heart in high school, and I feel really bad about it.

jokes.text: Waitress: 'You're making all of that up.' Dee: 'Really? Oh, no, no. You're absolutely right. I'm confusing you with another pathetic drunk that I know.'
jokes.setup: The waitress calls out Dee's fabrications
jokes.punchline: Dee 'apologizes' by claiming she confused the waitress with 'another pathetic drunk' — a fake retraction that's also an insult
jokes.explanation: 'Another pathetic drunk that I know' as a 'correction' is sharp — Dee's attempt to walk back the lie results in another insult. Character-specific and well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: Yeah, I sat right next to you in Trig.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Huh. Wow, you are very forgettable.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis are preparing Charlie for his date with a lawyer: 'This chick's a lawyer. She's gonna be pretty sharp.' Charlie is visibly sweating through his shirt.
jokes.setup: Mac is briefing Charlie on the date, emphasizing she's a lawyer and smart
jokes.punchline: Charlie is so nervous he's visibly sweating through his shirt before even meeting her — his body literally betraying him
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy setup — Charlie's physical anxiety is a good visual gag. 'He's sweating through his shirt, dude' is functional setup for the cheese joke to follow.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: How many people in the room have... had sex with the bride to be?

dialogue.speaker: Brad
dialogue.line: Uh, just me i hope.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Whoops.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Nuh uh.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Over here guy.

jokes.text: In the restaurant bathroom: Mac discovers Charlie has eaten an entire block of cheese because he was nervous. 'How much cheese is too much cheese?' 'Any amount of cheese before a date is too much cheese!' 'I had a lot of cheese. I had a block of cheese.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis find Charlie in the bathroom before the date — he was nervous
jokes.punchline: Charlie, faced with pre-date anxiety, ate an entire block of cheese. The specificity ('a block') and the exchange about acceptable cheese quantities is the joke
jokes.explanation: Very strong Charlie joke. 'I had a block of cheese' as a nervous-eating confession is specific and character-perfect — not just 'some cheese' but a whole block. 'Any amount of cheese before a date is too much cheese!' is a quotable line in its own right. Dennis's escalating questions about cheese quantity are well-paced. Only Charlie would eat a block of cheese before a date due to nerves.

dialogue.speaker: Mrs. Mac
dialogue.line: She's in love with my brother, they have a sex tape together, this guy came along I used to look like her. Gimme me my cigarettes. Everybody's stealing my Charlie!

jokes.text: Dee's 'newlywed game' first question: 'Who broke Brad's heart in high school and feels really bad about it?' — then answers her own question out loud
jokes.setup: Dee announces a 'newlywed-type game' for the party
jokes.punchline: The first question is transparently self-serving — it exists only to introduce Dee as Brad's ex in front of the waitress — and she answers it herself with zero pretense of it being a game
jokes.explanation: The 'game' as a barely-disguised self-promotion vehicle is a good cringe setup. Dee announcing 'Me. I broke Brad's heart in high school and I feel really bad about it. Okay?' is both pathetic and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I still love you.

jokes.text: The Waitress: 'You went to high school with us? I sat right next to you in trig.' Waitress: 'Huh! You are very forgettable.'
jokes.setup: Dee announces she went to their high school and sat next to the waitress in trig
jokes.punchline: The waitress has no memory of her whatsoever and says so bluntly: 'You are very forgettable'
jokes.explanation: 'You are very forgettable' is delivered with a casualness that makes it land harder than an aggressive insult would. The economy is excellent — four words that do maximum damage to Dee's self-importance.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: These are hornet's stings, you know? I run into a lot of hornets in my line of work, i got stung up bad all over my face.... then it starts bleeding.

jokes.text: Mrs. Mac blurts out: 'Both you girls dumped him because of his pizza face.'
jokes.setup: Dee has just awkwardly claimed she also broke Brad's heart; the party tension is building
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Mac delivers her scripted line with no social filter — 'pizza face' in front of Brad — detonating any remaining pretense of a normal party
jokes.explanation: 'Pizza face' said directly to/about Brad in a social setting by an elderly woman with no self-awareness is good dark comedy. The chaos it detonates earns it.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I'm a... full-on rapist. You know? Africans, dyslexics, children, that sort of thing.

jokes.text: Dee's second party game question: 'How many people in the room have had sex with the bride-to-be?' — Charlie's hand goes up
jokes.setup: Dee's 'game' escalates; she asks who has slept with the waitress
jokes.punchline: Charlie's hand goes up — the gang's resident stalker has apparently had sex with the waitress at some point, which is both shocking and terrible
jokes.explanation: Strong visual/reaction joke — the structure of the question makes Brad the expected answer ('just me, I hope'), then Charlie's hand raises. The 'Ew' from someone in the room is the perfect button. Rewatch bonus because knowing the Charlie/waitress dynamic makes it land differently.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Africans, dyslexics, children, that sort of thing.

jokes.text: Mac's mom explains the waitress's history: 'She's in love with my brother. They have a sex tape together. This guy came along—' then proudly: 'I used to look like her. Give me my cigarettes.'
jokes.setup: Mrs. Mac is supposed to say the waitress looks like her when she was young
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Mac delivers her scripted line mid-chaos, referencing a sex tape, then demands her cigarette payment — completing her paid contract with zero regard for the social disaster unfolding
jokes.explanation: Mrs. Mac's transactional compliance — completing her scripted line mid-chaos and immediately demanding payment — is a solid payoff on the cigarette setup. 'I used to look like her. Give me my cigarettes.' is funny as a complete thought.

dialogue.speaker: Jackie
dialogue.line: A philanthropist? Yeah! That's exactly what it is.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: It gets blocked up in my mouth, I don't say it no goods.

jokes.text: Mrs. Kelly: 'Everybody's stealing my Charlie, girl!' — attacks someone (implied physical confrontation)
jokes.setup: The party has devolved into chaos; Dee is getting attacked from multiple fronts
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Kelly, primed by Dee to be protective of Charlie, launches into a full maternal rage attack — a chaos agent Dee created but can't control
jokes.explanation: Mrs. Kelly's protective outburst lands as physical comedy and chaos escalation. 'Everybody's stealing my Charlie, girl!' is both funny as a line and as payoff on the setup.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: There was a guy in the bathroom, he wouldn't give me his shirt... and i was fightin' him. I was like, 'Gimme your shirt bro'. And he didn't want to give it to me and it was like a whole thing...

jokes.text: Frank to Artemis after the party collapses: 'This is depressing. Want to go get sweaty in the bathroom?' Artemis: 'Sure do.'
jokes.setup: The party has imploded; everyone is yelling
jokes.punchline: Frank's response to witnessing social catastrophe is an immediate pivot to sex in a bathroom — and Artemis agrees without hesitation
jokes.explanation: Frank's total indifference to everyone's distress, redirected immediately to his own gratification, is very character-specific. 'Sure do' from Artemis is a perfect deadpan affirmation — no hesitation, no reaction to the chaos. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: There was a guy in the bathroom, he wouldn't give me his shirt... and i was fightin' him. I was like, 'Gimme your shirt bro'.

jokes.text: Dee screams 'No one's getting sweaty in my bathroom!' — Frank: 'We'll go get sweaty in a Wendy's bathroom.' Artemis: 'Great!'
jokes.setup: Dee refuses to let Frank and Artemis use her bathroom for sex
jokes.punchline: Frank immediately pivots to Wendy's as the alternative venue, delivered as practically as 'we'll try the other bathroom' — and Artemis is enthusiastic about it
jokes.explanation: Wendy's as a sex venue is a great specific choice — not just 'a fast food restaurant' but Wendy's, which is funnier than McDonald's or Burger King for some ineffable reason. The escalation from 'my bathroom' to 'Wendy's bathroom' with Frank's total equanimity is excellent. 'Great!' from Artemis is perfect. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Now i'm gonna want the milksteak boiled over hard... and a side of your finest jellybeans, raw.

jokes.text: Dee screams at departing guests about 'condiments' and 'anything else you two want to jam up into each other's...' (cut off)
jokes.setup: The party has fully collapsed; everyone is leaving
jokes.punchline: Dee's farewell is a screaming rant about condiments that dissolves into an unfinished reference to what Frank and Artemis do with them sexually — the specificity of 'condiments' as the thing she's protecting recalls the food fetish setup
jokes.explanation: The cut-off line implies something worse than what's said — a good use of implication. The condiment callback adds a layer for attentive viewers.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: What does 'make a move' mean?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: It doesn't mean stab at her breast with your fingers.

jokes.text: Charlie shows up at Dee's door after the party chaos: 'I forgot to tell you... I still love you.' — addressed to the Waitress
jokes.setup: The party is in ruins; Dee is screaming at everyone to leave
jokes.punchline: Charlie, oblivious to the entire catastrophe, arrives to deliver a sincere romantic declaration to the waitress — the most inappropriate possible timing, with no awareness of what just happened
jokes.explanation: Charlie's sincere 'I still love you' dropped into a chaos scene he didn't witness — with a beat of silence before it — is well-executed character cringe. The timing (long pause after 'I forgot something') and the simplicity of the declaration make it land. Character-specific to Charlie's hopeless, oblivious romanticism.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You're grabbing her breast? What are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I don't know! What does 'make a move' mean?

jokes.text: Charlie arrives bleeding at the date — 'Oh, this? I was running.' — Jackie: 'Because you're bleeding.' Charlie: 'Oh, shit. Is it bleeding again?'
jokes.setup: Charlie arrives late to his date covered in hornet-sting wounds that are now bleeding
jokes.punchline: 'Oh, this? I was running' as an explanation for bleeding, followed by 'Is it bleeding again?' — suggesting this is a recurring problem
jokes.explanation: 'Is it bleeding again?' implies this is routine for Charlie — a callback to his earlier hornet battle that naturalizes his suffering. 'I was running' as the cover story for facial wounds is a good deflection line.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Guess what, bro? The waitress is getting married, so suck on that!

jokes.text: Charlie explains his job: 'I'm work- I'm like a janitor at, um... I'm a full-on rapist, you know? Uh, Africans, dyslexics, children, that sort of thing.'
jokes.setup: Jackie asks what Charlie does for work after he tried to say 'philanthropist'
jokes.punchline: Charlie's attempt at 'philanthropist' comes out as 'full-on rapist' — with 'Africans, dyslexics, children' as the stated victims (corruption of 'who I help as a philanthropist') — an accidental construction of the most alarming possible self-description
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode and one of the funniest moments in Sunny's run. The structure is impeccable: (1) the word 'philanthropist' was established as difficult to say, (2) Dennis's coaching included 'old people, children, autistics, dyslexic folks,' (3) Charlie's corruption of 'phil-anthropist' into 'rapist' and his parroting of Dennis's list of demographics creates the accidentally horrifying confession. The joke works on multiple levels: as a callback, as a character joke about Charlie's scrambled brain under pressure, and as pure shock comedy. 'That sort of thing' as the casual button is perfect. Among the best-structured jokes in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Well, i suppose i'll be taking that milksteak to go then.

jokes.text: Jackie: 'I'm sorry, did you say you're a full-on rapist?' Charlie: 'No! Did I say that? No! No, no, no, no!'
jokes.setup: Charlie has just accidentally described himself as a 'full-on rapist'
jokes.punchline: Jackie's calm, clarifying question and Charlie's panicked denial — 'Did I say that?' when he demonstrably just said it
jokes.explanation: Good reaction beat extending joke 52's impact. 'Did I say that?' when he clearly did is an effective comedic denial. Jackie's calm 'I'm sorry, did you say...' makes it land harder by not overplaying it.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: It's your hamburger, you clean that up. And then Artemis got all bombed-out because of something i did with the onions to myself.

jokes.text: Charlie gives up on 'philanthropist' and just says: 'I'm a janitor at a bar.'
jokes.setup: Charlie has tried and failed to say 'philanthropist' multiple times
jokes.punchline: He simply admits the truth — 'I'm a janitor at a bar' — delivered with the deflated resignation of someone who has just described himself as a rapist and needs to course-correct
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — five words that puncture all pretense. After 'full-on rapist' and failed 'philanthropist' attempts, the flat truth is the funniest possible statement. Well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Brad
dialogue.line: I've been getting engaged all these chicks who broke up with me at high school, because of my acne, and then i dump them right before the wedding.

jokes.text: 'I'm a janitor at a bar.' (Charlie finally admits the truth after failing to say 'philanthropist')
jokes.setup: After multiple failed attempts at 'philanthropist' — landing on 'rapist' and stumbling through the syllables — Charlie tries one more time
jokes.punchline: He simply gives up and tells the truth: 'I'm a janitor at a bar.' — the honesty landing like a confession
jokes.explanation: Five words that land perfectly after the chaos of the 'rapist' disaster. The deflation from 'philanthropist' to 'janitor at a bar' is a great structural collapse. Maximum economy — this is the actual truth stripped of all pretension. Very well deployed.

dialogue.speaker: Brad
dialogue.line: Yeah. Yeah. She was devistated.

jokes.text: 'Oh, God, dude! I'm sucking ass!' — Charlie's self-assessment from offscreen/in bathroom
jokes.setup: Charlie has just had his worst possible first impression
jokes.punchline: Charlie's private self-assessment — 'I'm sucking ass!' — is both accurate and funny as a callback to Dennis and Mac monitoring from nearby
jokes.explanation: Functional transition joke — Charlie's accurate self-awareness (expressed in crude terms) bridges the rapist disaster to the bathroom rescue. Not exceptional but lands.

jokes.text: In the restaurant bathroom: Dennis and Mac debriefing Charlie; Mac tries to give Dennis his shirt so Charlie can wear it; Dennis refuses. Charlie: 'I'll say I met a nice guy in the bathroom and we traded shirts!'
jokes.setup: Charlie's shirt is ruined (blood, sweat); he wants Dennis's shirt
jokes.punchline: Charlie's proposed explanation for a shirt change — 'I met a nice guy in the bathroom and we traded' — is so implausible it loops around to being the worst possible cover story
jokes.explanation: Charlie's earnest suggestion of the most suspicious possible cover story is very Charlie — he genuinely thinks this is a good plan. 'Are you listening to yourself?' from Dennis captures the audience's reaction perfectly.

jokes.text: Mac's dating advice: 'Charlie, make a move. Just tell her you want to bang her.' Dennis: 'No, that's—' Mac: 'He's got a 50-50 shot.' Dennis: 'That's a good point! It is a yes-or-no scenario.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are debating how to save the date
jokes.punchline: Mac's catastrophically bad advice ('just tell her you want to bang her') is initially rejected by Dennis, but then Dennis's logic ('it's a 50-50 shot / yes-or-no scenario') convinces them both it's reasonable
jokes.explanation: Dennis applying game-theory logic ('50-50 shot, yes-or-no scenario') to validate terrible advice is excellent character work for both Mac and Dennis. The escalation of Dennis going from 'No, that's—' to 'That's a good point!' in one breath is well-structured.

jokes.text: Dennis walks out as 'the manager of Gugino's' in an absurd cover identity: 'Mr. Kelly is one of our preferred customers... he has the most wonderful sense of humor'
jokes.setup: Dennis has established a 'manager' cover story to rescue Charlie's date
jokes.punchline: Dennis's 'manager' performance is a masterclass in condescending fakery — praising Charlie's 'milk steak' order as a 'wonderful sense of humor' while trying to cover for it
jokes.explanation: Dennis's smooth, sociopathic 'manager' performance is good character work. The milk steak callback — reframed as humor rather than a real order — adds a layer.

jokes.text: Charlie, playing along with Dennis's manager bit, orders 'milk steak boiled over hard and a side of your finest jellybeans, raw'
jokes.setup: Dennis has established himself as the restaurant manager to legitimize Charlie
jokes.punchline: Charlie, supposedly playing the role of a wealthy, respectable customer, orders milk steak AND jellybeans raw — doubling down on his real preferences rather than playing along
jokes.explanation: The milk steak callback in the worst possible context is structurally perfect. Dennis just told Jackie the order was a joke — then Charlie immediately places the same order for real, plus 'finest jellybeans, raw.' 'Raw' as the modifier for jellybeans (which are already a candy and cannot be meaningfully 'raw') is an inspired addition. The escalation from just 'milk steak' to 'milk steak boiled over hard and a side of your finest jellybeans, raw' makes it funnier than the original. Among the episode's best moments.

jokes.text: Dennis, as 'manager': 'Hey, I own this joint and I know this guy and he is loaded.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is trying to rehabilitate Charlie's image after the milk steak order
jokes.punchline: Dennis's 'manager' performance devolves to just asserting Charlie is rich — the thinnest possible cover for a man covered in hornet stings who just ordered milk steak
jokes.explanation: Functional extension of the Dennis-manager bit. 'He is loaded' is a classic non-specific rich claim that nobody would believe given the visible evidence.

jokes.text: Dennis-as-manager suggests: 'How's about I clear out the coat room and you guys hit it in there while the steak is getting ready?'
jokes.setup: Dennis is supposedly helping Charlie's date go well
jokes.punchline: Dennis's 'help' devolves to suggesting the couple go have sex in the coat room immediately — which is both deeply inappropriate and reveals Dennis's own approach to seduction
jokes.explanation: Dennis's coat room suggestion — presented as helpful 'management' — exposes his own grotesque approach to romance. Character-specific and well-executed.

jokes.text: Mac shouts 'Charlie, make a move. Maul.' — Charlie grabs Jackie's breasts. 'You're grabbing her breasts? What are you doing?' Charlie: 'I don't know. What does "make a move" mean?'
jokes.setup: Mac's advice was to 'make a move'; Charlie is interpreting this instruction literally and incorrectly
jokes.punchline: Charlie interprets 'make a move' as grabbing her breasts — his genuine question 'What does "make a move" mean?' shows he has no social framework for this whatsoever
jokes.explanation: 'What does make a move mean?' is a great Charlie line — his genuine ignorance of basic social norms, expressed as a sincere question after a sexual assault, is horrifying and funny in the specific way Sunny executes dark comedy. The earlier setup (Mac coaching Charlie) makes the payoff land harder. Dennis's 'It doesn't mean stab at her breasts with your fingers' as a correction is an excellent button.

jokes.text: Dennis breaks the news: 'Guess what, bro. The waitress is getting married. So suck on that!'
jokes.setup: Charlie has blamed Mac and Dennis for the failed date
jokes.punchline: Dennis retaliates by revealing the waitress's engagement — deliberately weaponizing information to hurt Charlie, punctuated with 'So suck on that!' which is oddly childish
jokes.explanation: 'So suck on that!' from Dennis is a great childish button on what should be devastating news. Dennis weaponizing the information out of pettiness rather than any strategic reason is character-perfect.

jokes.text: Charlie's response to learning the waitress is getting married: a long pause, then 'Well, I suppose I'll be taking that milk steak to go then.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has just told Charlie the woman he's obsessed with is getting married — potentially devastating news
jokes.punchline: Charlie processes this life-changing information and his only response is to pivot to his food order — 'milk steak to go' — with the quiet dignity of a man who has decided to hold it together
jokes.explanation: Among the best jokes in the episode. The structure is near-perfect: devastating emotional reveal → long silence → Charlie responds not with grief but with the most mundane, food-related non-sequitur possible. The callback to 'milk steak' as the vehicle for Charlie's emotional response is structurally brilliant — it simultaneously caps the milk steak running gag AND delivers a surprisingly poignant character beat. 'I suppose I'll be taking that milk steak to go then' has the cadence of a man maintaining dignity in the face of heartbreak, but the content is absurdist nonsense. Genuinely exceptional writing.

jokes.text: Frank describes a Wendy's incident to Dee: 'So the Wendy's manager is all, "You gotta clean that up!" And I said, "They're your hamburgers. You clean 'em up." And then Artemis got all bummed out because of something I did with the onions to myself.'
jokes.setup: Frank and Artemis apparently just had sex at Wendy's (as promised); Frank is debriefing Dee
jokes.punchline: The sexual encounter at Wendy's involved the hamburgers and specifically 'something he did with the onions to himself' — the vagueness implying something much worse than stated
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback payoff on the Wendy's threat. 'Something I did with the onions to myself' as the specific detail that disturbed even Artemis (who is not easily disturbed) is perfectly constructed — the implication is funnier than any explicit description. Frank's matter-of-fact delivery and his genuine grievance about whose responsibility the cleanup is adds another layer.

jokes.text: The gang preparing to arm themselves with a baseball bat because Charlie might 'go postal' — then Frank says 'Oh, don't worry about Charlie. Charlie's over this.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are grabbing a baseball bat because they expect Charlie to show up and potentially attack them
jokes.punchline: Frank casually dismisses their fear with 'Charlie's over this' — which turns out to be both true and also reveals that Frank has information they don't, delivered with his usual breezy indifference to danger
jokes.explanation: The gang arming themselves against Charlie is a good dark beat — it confirms what we knew about Charlie's volatility. Frank's dismissal sets up the reveal about Brad. Functional but minor.

jokes.text: Frank: 'Oh, don't worry about Charlie. Charlie's over this. In fact, I saw him this morning. He said he was bringing the guy a congratulatory gift.'
jokes.setup: Mac is grabbing a baseball bat to arm himself against a potentially violent Charlie
jokes.punchline: Frank dismisses the concern with the information that Charlie is 'bringing a congratulatory gift' — which could either mean Charlie is genuinely fine OR that it's a trap/weapon
jokes.explanation: Setup beat for the final scene. The 'congratulatory gift' is intentionally ambiguous — audience isn't sure whether to trust it. Functional but not funny on its own.

jokes.text: Charlie arrives at Brad's door with a gift box, buzzing faintly. 'This is for your engagement, man. You're a lucky, lucky dude.'
jokes.setup: Charlie has brought a 'congratulatory gift' to Brad; the box is making a faint buzzing sound
jokes.punchline: The box is buzzing — the audience immediately understands it's the hornet nest marked with 'H' — but the reveal is held as Brad accepts it with thanks
jokes.explanation: Structurally satisfying — the hornet nest subplot pays off as Charlie's 'gift.' 'You're a lucky, lucky dude' has a double meaning (Brad is unaware of what 'luck' awaits him). The callback to the H-marked box is a clean, well-earned payoff.

jokes.text: Brad tells Charlie: he's been getting revenge on women who dumped him for acne by getting engaged to them and dumping them right before the wedding. He's just done it to the waitress, and next is 'Dee Reynolds. Remember her? She was the worst.'
jokes.setup: Brad has just revealed he's not actually getting married — it's all been a revenge scheme
jokes.punchline: The waitress's marriage was always fake — Brad is a systematic revenge-dater who has been doing this for years, and Dee is next — a complete structural inversion of everything the episode set up
jokes.explanation: Major structural reveal that retroactively reframes the entire episode. The acne backstory introduced in the cold open becomes the motivation for a seasons-long revenge scheme. 'She was the worst' about Dee lands especially well because we've just watched 20 minutes of evidence for that claim. This is the episode's macro-level joke — all of the gang's scheming and suffering was in response to something that wasn't even real.

jokes.text: Charlie gives Brad the gift — a buzzing box that is clearly the hornets nest labeled 'H'
jokes.setup: Charlie has brought a 'congratulatory gift' for Brad; he hands it over with a friendly 'that's rad'
jokes.punchline: The buzzing from the box and the 'H' label reveal it's the hornets nest — Charlie's revenge gift is the same hornets nest that has been stinging him all episode, now gifted to the man who broke the Waitress's heart
jokes.explanation: The perfect episode closer and arguably the best structural joke in the episode. Every element was seeded — the hornets nest, the 'H' label, Charlie's acceptance of pain, Brad's cruelty — and they snap together into an ending that is simultaneously absurd and darkly poetic. Charlie's revenge is proportional, wordless, and brilliant. The 'That's rad' / 'All right. Well, keep it real, man' normalcy of the exchange while handing over a buzzing box of hornets is exquisite deadpan. This is Sunny at its structural best — a callback that works on a character level and a plot level simultaneously. Comparable to the anchor examples in craft.

jokes.text: Post-scene: faint buzzing sound, then Charlie chuckling as he walks away
jokes.setup: Brad has just accepted the hornet nest
jokes.punchline: The faint buzzing from inside Brad's apartment begins as Charlie walks away laughing — the audience understands what's happening without seeing it
jokes.explanation: Clean, economic visual/audio coda. The buzzing implies hornet chaos off-screen; Charlie's chuckle is the perfect final note for his character's arc. Very economical — no dialogue needed.

tmdb_overview: The waitress is getting married, Dee is jealous that she's beating her to the altar, so she tries to derail the wedding.
